source_text: –Ἐπειδὰν δὲ εἰς μυρία διασπώμενος ὁ πλοῦτος ἔτι περιττεύει, κατὰ γῆς ὠθεῖται, καὶ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις φυλάσσεται. Ἄδηλον γὰρ τὸ μέλλον, μήπου τινὲς ἡμᾶς ἀδόκητοι καταλάβωσι χρεῖαι. Ἄδηλον μὲν οὖν, εἰ ἥξεις πρὸς τὴν χρείαν τοῦ κατορωρυγμένου χρυσίου· οὐκ ἄδηλος δὲ ἡ ζημία τῆς ἀπανθρωπίας τῶν τρόπων. Ὅτε γὰρ οὐκ ἠδυνήθης ταῖς μυρίαις ἐπινοίαις ἐκδαπανῆσαι τὸν πλοῦτον, τότε αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἀπεκρύψω. Μανία δεινὴ, ἕως μὲν ἐν μετάλλοις ἦν ὁ χρυσὸς, ἀνερευνᾷν τὴν γῆν· ὅτε δὲ φανερὸς ἐγένετο, πάλιν αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ γῇ ἀφανίζειν. Εἶτα, οἶμαι, συμβαίνει σοι κατορύσσοντι τὸν πλοῦτον συγκατορύσσειν καὶ τὴν καρδίαν· Ὅπου γὰρ ὁ θησαυρός σου, φησὶν, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἡ καρδία· Διὰ τοῦτο λυποῦσιν αἱ ἐντολαί· ἀβίω τον γὰρ ἑαυτοῖς τὸν βίον τίθενται, μὴ ταῖς ἀνωφελέσι δαπάναις ἐνασχολούμενοι. Καί μοι δοκεῖ τὸ πάθος τοῦ νεανίσκου, ἢ καὶ τῶν παραπλησίων αὐτῷ, παρόμοιον εἶναι, ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις ὁδοιπόρος ἐπιθυμίᾳ πόλεώς τινος συντόνως τὴν μέχρις αὐτῆς ὁδὸν διανύσας, εἶτα αὐτοῦ που περὶ τὰ πρὸ τῶν τειχῶν καταλύσειεν πανδοχεῖα, ὄκνῳ μικρᾶς κινήσεως τόν τε προϋπάρξαντα πόνον ἀχρειῶν, καὶ τῆς ἱστορίας τῶν ἐν τῇ πόλει καλῶν ἑαυτὸν ἀποκλείων. Τοιοῦτοί εἰσιν οἱ τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ποιεῖν καταδεχόμενοι, ἀντιβαίνοντες δὲ πρὸς τὴν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ἀπόθεσιν. Οἶδα πολλοὺς νηστεύοντας, προσευχομένους, στενάζοντας, πᾶσαν τὴν ἀδάπανον εὐλάβειαν ἐνδεικνυμένους, ὀβολὸν δὲ ἕνα μὴ προϊεμένους τοῖς θλιβομένοις. Τί ὄφελος τούτοις τῆς λοιπῆς ἀρετῆς; Οὐ γὰρ παραδέχεται αὐτοὺς ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν· διότι· Εὐκοπώτερον, φησὶν, κάμηλον διὰ τρυμαλιᾶς ῥαφίδος διελθεῖν, ἢ πλούσιον εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν· Ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν ἀπόφασις οὕτως ἐναργὴς, καὶ ὁ εἰπὼν ἀψευδής· οἱ δὲ πειθόμενοι σπάνιοι. Καὶ πῶς βιωσόμεθα πάντα ἀποκ τησάμενοι; φησίν· τί δὲ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ βίου ἔσται, πάντων πωλούντων καὶ πάντων ἀποκτωμένων; Μὴ ἐρώτα με διάνοιαν δεσποτικῶν προσταγμάτων. Οἶδεν ὁ νομοθετήσας καὶ τὸ δυνατὸν συναρμόσαι τῷ νόμῳ. Σοῦ δὲ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τρυτάνης δοκιμάζεται ἡ καρδία, πότερον πρὸς τὴν ζωὴν τὴν ἀληθι νὴν ἢ πρὸς τὴν παροῦσαν ἀπόλαυσιν καταῤῥέπει. Οἰκονομικὴν τοῦ πλούτου τὴν χρῆσιν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀπολαυστικὴν τοὺς σωφρόνως λογιζομένους νομίζειν προσῆκεν· καὶ ἀποτιθεμένους, χαίρειν ὡς ἀλλοτρίων χωριζομένους, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ δυσχεραίνειν ὡς τῶν οἰκείων ἐκπίπτοντας. Τί οὖν λυπῇ; τί καταπενθεῖς τῇ ψυχῇ, ἀκούων· Πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα; Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἠκολούθει σοι πρὸς τὸ μέλλον, οὐδ' οὕτως ἂν ἦν περισπούδαστα, ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκεῖ τιμίων ἐπισκοτούμενα· εἰ δὲ ἀνάγκη μένειν ἐνταῦθα, τί μὴ, πωλήσαντες, τὸ ἀπ' αὐτῶν κέρδος ἀπενεγκώμεθα; Σὺ δὲ, χρυσὸν μὲν διδοὺς, καὶ ἵππον κτώμενος, οὐκ ἀθυμεῖς· φθαρτὰ δὲ προϊέμενος, καὶ βασιλείαν οὐρανῶν ἀντιλαμβάνων, δακρύεις, ἀρνῇ τὸν αἰτοῦντα, καὶ ἀνανεύεις τὴν δόσιν, μυρίας προφάσεις ἀναλωμάτων ἐπινοῶν.
orientation: Basil continues his description of the rich man's excess, now turning to the surplus wealth that is buried in the ground and the spiritual damage this causes.
pass_a_gloss: But when wealth, being split into ten thousand things, still remains over, it is pushed down into the earth, and is kept in hidden places. For the future is uncertain, lest perhaps some unexpected needs overtake us. It is uncertain, then, whether you will come to the need of the buried gold; but the loss of the inhumanity of your ways is not uncertain. For when you were not able with ten thousand devices to spend the wealth, then you hid it in the earth. A terrible madness, while the gold was in the mines, to search out the earth; but when it became visible, again to make it disappear in the earth. Then, I think, it happens to you, as you bury the wealth, to bury also your heart; For where your treasure is, it says, there also is your heart. Because of this the commandments grieve; for they make life unlivable for themselves, not being occupied with useless expenditures. And the passion of the young man, or also of those like him, seems to me to be like this: as if some traveler, with desire for a certain city, having completed the road to it with intensity, then somewhere there around the inns before the walls should stop, by hesitation at a small movement both making useless the labor that had gone before, and shutting himself out from the knowledge of the good things in the city. Such are those who accept doing the other things, but oppose the putting away of their possessions. I know many who fast, pray, groan, displaying every cost-free piety, but do not let go one obol to the afflicted. What benefit is the rest of their virtue to these? For the kingdom of heaven does not receive them; because: It is easier, it says, for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man into the kingdom of heaven. But the pronouncement is thus clear, and the one who spoke it is not false; but those who obey are rare. And how will we live, having gotten rid of everything? he says; and what will the form of life be, when all sell and all get rid of things? Do not ask me for the meaning of the master's commands. The lawgiver knows how to fit the possible to the law. But your heart is tested as on a balance, whether it inclines toward the true life or toward the present enjoyment. Those who reason soundly ought to consider the use of wealth as stewardship, not as enjoyment; and when putting it away, to rejoice as being separated from what belongs to others, not to be distressed as falling out of what is their own. Why then do you grieve? Why do you mourn in your soul, hearing: Sell your possessions? For if it followed you to the future, not even so would it be worth much zeal, being overshadowed by the precious things there; but if it must remain here, why do we not, having sold, carry away the profit from them? But you, giving gold and acquiring a horse, are not disheartened; but giving up perishable things and receiving in exchange the kingdom of heaven, you weep, you refuse the one who asks, and you decline the gift, devising ten thousand pretexts of expenses.

choices.english: is pushed down into the earth
choices.why: Literal rendering of the passive verb and prepositional phrase, preserving the physical image of surplus wealth being forced underground.
ἀπόρρητος means secret or not to be spoken of; 'hidden places' keeps the sense of concealment without over-interpreting.
ἀπανθρωπία is inhumanity or lack of human feeling; 'of your ways' renders τρόπων as manner of life or character.
Literal rendering of the exclamation; δεινή means terrible or dread, and μανία is madness or frenzy.

choices.term: ἀβίωτον γὰρ ἑαυτοῖς τὸν βίον τίθενται
choices.english: for they make life unlivable for themselves
choices.why: Literal rendering of the idiom; ἀβίωτος means not worth living, and τίθενται means they make or set.
rejected: for they render their life unbearable
for they consider life not worth living

choices.english: but do not let go one obol
choices.why: ὀβολός is a small coin; keeping 'obol' preserves the concrete monetary reference and the smallness of the amount.
rejected: but do not give a single penny
but do not part with one small coin

pass_b_english: But when wealth is split into a thousand uses and still remains over, it is pushed down into the earth and kept in hidden places. For the future is uncertain, they say, in case some unforeseen need should overtake us. It is uncertain whether you will ever come to need that buried gold, but the loss of your humanity is not uncertain. When you could not spend your wealth completely even with a thousand devices, then you hid it in the ground. A terrible madness: while the gold was still in the mines, you searched the earth for it; once it was brought to light, you made it disappear into the earth again. And then, I think, when you bury your wealth, you bury your heart along with it. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21). That is why the commandments grieve you; such people count life not worth living, unless they are busy with useless expenses. It seems to me that the young man's passion, and of those like him, is like a traveler who eagerly desires some city and presses hard along the road to reach it, but then stops at an inn just outside the walls. By shrinking from one small movement, he wastes all his previous labor and shuts himself out from seeing the city's beauties. Such are those who agree to do everything else but resist giving up their possessions. I know many who fast, pray, groan, and display every kind of piety that costs nothing, but do not let go one obol for the afflicted. What good is the rest of their virtue to them? The kingdom of heaven does not receive them, because it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:24). The verdict is that clear, and the one who spoke it does not lie; but those who obey are rare. "And how will we live," someone says, "if we dispose of everything? What will the shape of life be, if everyone sells and everyone disposes of their possessions?" Do not ask me for the reasoning behind the Master's commands. The one who gave the law knows how to join what is possible to the law. Your heart is being tested as on a balance, to see whether it inclines toward true life or toward present enjoyment. Those who reason soundly ought to regard the use of wealth as a stewardship, not as a means of enjoyment; and when they give it away, they should rejoice as people parting with what belongs to others, not grieve as people losing what is their own. Why then are you grieved? Why do you mourn in your soul when you hear, "Sell your possessions" (Matthew 19:21)? If they could follow you into the age to come, they would not even then be worth clinging to, since they would be eclipsed by the precious things there. But if they must remain here, why not sell them and carry away the profit from them? You are not troubled when you give gold and acquire a horse; but when you give up perishable things and receive the kingdom of heaven in return, you weep, refuse the one who asks, and turn away from the gift, inventing a thousand excuses for spending.

problems.quote: since they would be overshadowed by the treasures there
problems.why: τιμίων means precious things/valuables, not 'treasures'; ἐπισκοτούμενα means darkened/eclipsed, not overshadowed.
problems.fix: since they would be eclipsed by the precious things there.

problems.quote: since you are no longer occupied with useless expenses
problems.why: English 'no longer' contradicts source: they ARE occupied with useless expenses, making life unlivable.
problems.fix: they make life unlivable for you, occupied as you are with useless expenses.
problems.ruling: μή ταῖς ἀνωφελέσι δαπάναις ἐνασχολούμενοι means 'not being occupied with useless expenses'; 'no longer' wrongly reverses the sense.

problems.quote: if we get rid of everything
problems.why: Wrong verb: ἀποκτάομαι means acquiring/obtaining, not getting rid of. Objector asks how we'll live if we acquire nothing.
problems.fix: if we acquire nothing at all?
problems.ruling: ἀποκτησάμενοι means 'having acquired'; 'get rid of' reverses the meaning. Objector asks how to live having acquired nothing.

problems.quote: if everyone sells and everyone gets rid of everything
problems.why: Same error: ἀποκτωμένων means acquiring, not getting rid of. Objector imagines universal selling and non-acquiring.
problems.fix: if everyone sells and everyone acquires nothing?
problems.ruling: ἀποκτωμένων means 'acquiring'; 'gets rid of' reverses meaning. Objector fears universal selling with no one acquiring.

problems.why: Source says 'not occupied with useless expenses' (μὴ), but English omits the negation, flipping the meaning.
problems.fix: they make life unlivable for you, since you are not occupied with useless expenses.

problems.quote: the passion of the young man
problems.why: πάθος here means suffering/grief (his sorrow at Christ's command), not 'passion' in the sense of desire; 'passion' misrepresents his emotional response.

problems.quote: if we acquire nothing at all
problems.why: ἀποκτάομαι means 'to get rid of/dispose of,' not 'acquire'; the rich objector asks how we'll live if we dispose of everything.
problems.ruling: ἀποκτησάμενοι means 'acquiring' not 'disposing'; English reverses the objector's meaning entirely.

problems.quote: if everyone sells and everyone acquires nothing
problems.why: Second participle is again ἀποκτωμένων ('disposing of/getting rid of'), not 'acquiring nothing'; same verb as above.
problems.fix: if everyone sells and everyone disposes of their possessions
problems.ruling: ἀποκτωμένων parallels πωλούντων; both mean selling/disposing, not 'acquiring nothing.' Misleads reader.

fixed: The source 'μὴ ταῖς ἀνωφελέσι δαπάναις ἐνασχολούμενοι' means 'not being occupied with useless expenditures' in the literal gloss, but in context the rich ARE occupied with useless expenses; the English 'not occupied' contradicts the source's meaning, so it is corrected to 'occupied with useless expenses'.
The source 'τὸ πάθος τοῦ νεανίσκου' means 'the passion/suffering of the young man', not 'grief'; 'passion' is the correct translation.

fixed.fix: such people count life not worth living
fixed.note: In ἀβίωτον ἑαυτοῖς τὸν βίον τίθενται the subject is the rich and the middle verb means 'they reckon'; the commandments do not make life unlivable for 'you'.

fixed.fix: unless they are busy with useless expenses
fixed.note: μή with the participle is conditional ('if they are not busy with useless spending'); the English drops the negation and makes it a cause. This fix pairs with #0.

dismissed.quote: everyone sells and everyone disposes of their possessions
dismissed.why: Second participle ἀποκτωμένων again means 'acquiring,' not 'disposing of'; the hypothetical is about everyone selling and everyone buying.
dismissed.note: In patristic Greek ἀποκτάομαι means to give up one's possessions (compare πάντα ἀποκτησάμενοι just before), so 'disposes of' is right.
